title: The seventh seal, the golden censer and the first four trumpets
summary: The Lamb opens the seventh seal and heaven falls silent for about half an hour. Seven angels who stand before God receive seven trumpets, while another angel offers incense with the prayers of the saints on the golden altar and then hurls fire from that altar to the earth, setting off thunder, lightning and earthquake. The first four trumpets strike a third of the land, sea, fresh waters and heavenly lights in plagues modelled on the Exodus: hail and fire mixed with blood, a burning mountain thrown into the sea, a falling star named Wormwood, and darkness. An eagle in mid-heaven then announces three woes still to come on those who dwell on the earth.

outline.heading: The seventh seal: silence in heaven
Seven trumpets given; the prayers of the saints and the golden censer
First trumpet: hail and fire mixed with blood on the land
Second trumpet: a burning mountain cast into the sea
Third trumpet: the star Wormwood poisons the rivers
Fourth trumpet: a third of sun, moon and stars darkened
The eagle's threefold woe

context:
The chapter is built from the temple and from the Exodus. In the Second Temple the twice-daily Tamid offering was accompanied by the burning of incense on the golden altar inside the sanctuary, while the people prayed outside (Luke 1:9-10; Mishnah Tamid 5-7, a later codification of earlier practice); Levites sang and trumpets were blown at the climax of the service. John fuses that liturgy with the prayer of the martyrs under the altar (Revelation 6:9-11): the incense-prayer goes up, and judgment comes down. Trumpets (shofar or silver trumpets, Numbers 10:1-10) summoned Israel to assembly and to war, announced festivals and the Day of the Lord (Joel 2:1; Zephaniah 1:16), brought down Jericho after seven priests with seven trumpets circled it seven times (Joshua 6), and in apocalyptic texts herald the end (Isaiah 27:13; 4 Ezra 6:23; 1 Thessalonians 4:16). The first four trumpets track the plagues on Egypt (hail and fire, water to blood, darkness) but are limited to "a third", which most commentators take as partial, warning judgments short of the final bowls (Revelation 16), echoing the divided thirds of Ezekiel 5:2-12 and Zechariah 13:8-9.

For readers in Roman Asia the images carried local weight. The province lived by the sea trade that the second trumpet wrecks; the eruption of Vesuvius (AD 79), which some commentators think lies behind the burning mountain, was recent news if the book dates to c. 95, while those who date it before AD 70 point instead to Jeremiah 51:25 and the Jewish War. Eagles were the standards of the Roman legions, and in Jewish apocalyptic (4 Ezra 11-12) the eagle stood for Rome; here, however, an eagle is a herald of God. Whether the trumpets follow the seals chronologically or recapitulate them from another angle is one of the oldest debates on the book: Victorinus of Pettau (c. 260, the earliest surviving Latin commentary) already argued that the trumpets and bowls repeat the same events.

symbols.phrase: Silence in heaven for about half an hour
symbols.jewish: Silence before the Lord precedes his coming in judgment in Habakkuk 2:20, Zephaniah 1:7 and Zechariah 2:13. Jewish tradition also imagined the heavenly praise pausing so that Israel's prayers could be heard (a later rabbinic motif in the Babylonian Talmud, Hagigah 12b, and Genesis Rabbah); in temple practice the people prayed silently while the priest offered incense (Luke 1:10). 2 Baruch 3:7 and 4 Ezra 7:30 speak of a primeval silence returning before the new creation.
symbols.cultural: Ancient sacrifices and mystery rites often called for ritual silence (Greek euphemia, Latin favete linguis) so that ill-omened words would not spoil the offering.
symbols.meaning: A dramatic pause that marks the seventh seal as a hinge: the ceaseless worship of chapters 4-5 stops so that the saints' prayers in 8:3-5 are heard and judgment can begin. "Half an hour" signals a short, broken interval rather than a measurable period. Whether the seventh seal "contains" the seven trumpets (a telescoping structure) or brings the seal series to its end with the final judgment is debated.

readings.reading: A liturgical silence of awe before God's answer to prayer; it belongs to the repeating cycle of judgment and is not a datable moment.
A literal, ominous lull in heaven in the future Tribulation before the more severe trumpet judgments, which unfold out of the seventh seal.
Elliott and Barnes saw a brief lull after Theodosius and the Christian empire's settlement (late fourth century) before the barbarian invasions of the trumpets fell on the western empire.
The pause before the covenant judgments of the Jewish War (AD 66-70) fall on the land; Chilton links it to the silence of the people during the temple incense offering.

symbols.phrase: The seven angels who stand before God
symbols.jewish: The definite article points to a known group: the seven archangels of Second Temple angelology. Tobit 12:15 has Raphael call himself one of the seven angels who stand ready before the Lord's glory, and 1 Enoch 20 names seven (Uriel, Raphael, Raguel, Michael, Sariel, Gabriel, Remiel). Gabriel says he "stands before God" in Luke 1:19. "Standing before" is court and priestly language for ministers in attendance (1 Kings 17:1; Deuteronomy 10:8).
symbols.cultural: Royal and imperial courts had an inner circle of attendants with direct access to the ruler; seven-fold groupings also echoed the seven planetary powers of astrology, which Jewish writers subordinated to God.
symbols.meaning: High angelic ministers of the divine court who execute the trumpet judgments, showing that what follows is ordered from the throne, not random catastrophe.

symbols.phrase: Seven trumpets
symbols.jewish: Trumpets assembled Israel, sounded alarm for war and marked festivals (Numbers 10:1-10); Rosh Hashanah is the day of trumpet blasts (Leviticus 23:24). Seven priests with seven ram's-horn trumpets brought down Jericho (Joshua 6:4-20). The prophets use the trumpet for the Day of the Lord and for warning (Joel 2:1; Zephaniah 1:14-16; Ezekiel 33:3-6), and the great trumpet gathers the exiles (Isaiah 27:13). The Qumran War Scroll (1QM 2-3, 7-9) prescribes inscribed trumpets for each stage of the eschatological war.
symbols.cultural: Roman armies used the tuba and cornu to give signals in battle and on the march; trumpets also opened games and processions.
symbols.meaning: Heralds of holy war and warning. Their judgments are partial (a third) and aimed at prompting repentance (9:20-21), in contrast to the final bowls of chapter 16. The seventh trumpet (11:15) announces the kingdom and is often linked with the "last trumpet" of 1 Corinthians 15:52 and 1 Thessalonians 4:16, a link that is itself contested.

readings.reading: Seven sequential judgments in the future seven-year Tribulation, following the seals; dispensationalists (Walvoord, Thomas) generally deny that the seventh trumpet is the "last trumpet" of 1 Corinthians 15 because they place the rapture before the Tribulation.

A chronological series across church history: the first four against the western Roman Empire (Goths, Vandals, Huns, the fall of the western emperor in 476), the fifth and sixth against the eastern empire (Saracens and Turks).
The covenant-lawsuit alarm against apostate Jerusalem, sounding through the Jewish War; like Jericho, the "city" falls at the seventh blast.
Recurring warning judgments throughout the age between Christ's comings; the trumpets recapitulate the seals from a different angle and climax at the end.

symbols.phrase: Another angel with a golden censer at the altar
symbols.jewish: On the Day of Atonement the high priest took a censer full of coals from the altar and two handfuls of incense into the Holy of Holies (Leviticus 16:12-13); Hebrews 9:4 associates a golden censer with the inner sanctuary. Censers also carried atonement in Numbers 16:46-48, where Aaron stops a plague. Some Jewish traditions describe an angel (often Michael) offering the prayers of the righteous in heaven (Tobit 12:12, 15; 3 Baruch 11-16; Testament of Levi 3:5-6).
symbols.cultural: Incense burners were standard in Greco-Roman sacrifice and in the imperial cult, where incense offered before the emperor's image was a test of loyalty that Christians refused (Pliny, Letters 10.96).
symbols.meaning: An angel performs a priestly role in the heavenly temple, presenting the prayers of God's people. The question whether this "other angel" is Christ (as some older Protestant commentators held) is answered no by most modern interpreters, since Revelation never calls Christ an angel and here the angel only assists the saints' prayers.

readings.reading: Several historicists (e.g. Elliott) read the angel as Christ the true High Priest, contrasted with corrupt intercession of saints and clergy in the church of the fourth and fifth centuries.
Usually a created angel ministering in the heavenly temple in the Tribulation period.

symbols.phrase: Much incense with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar
symbols.jewish: The golden altar of incense stood before the veil in the Holy Place (Exodus 30:1-10; 40:5); incense was burned morning and evening with the daily sacrifice, the hour of prayer (Luke 1:9-10; Acts 3:1). Psalm 141:2 asks that prayer rise like incense. Revelation 5:8 has already identified bowls of incense as the saints' prayers, and 6:9-11 placed the martyrs' cry for vindication under the altar.
symbols.cultural: Incense (frankincense from Arabia) was costly and burned in pagan temples and at imperial ceremonies; in Asia, Christians would have recognised the contrast with offering incense to Caesar.
symbols.meaning: The trumpet judgments are presented as God's answer to his people's prayers, especially the martyrs' plea "How long?" (6:10). Prayer is not passive: it is part of the means by which God governs history.

symbols.phrase: The censer filled with altar fire and hurled to the earth
symbols.jewish: Modelled on Ezekiel 10:2-7, where a man in linen takes coals from between the cherubim and scatters them over Jerusalem as a sign of its coming destruction. Fire from the altar elsewhere signifies divine judgment (Leviticus 10:1-2; Isaiah 6:6-7 for its purifying side).
symbols.meaning: The same altar that receives prayer becomes the source of judgment: the saints' prayers are answered by fire cast on the earth. The reversal of the censer's direction (up as incense, down as fire) is the theological centre of the chapter.

readings.reading: Because Ezekiel 10 concerns the burning of Jerusalem, preterists such as Chilton see the echo as a signal that the coming judgments target the same city in AD 70.
A pattern of judgment answering the persecuted church's prayers in every era.

symbols.phrase: Thunder, rumblings, lightning and an earthquake
symbols.jewish: The Sinai theophany formula (Exodus 19:16-18) with storm, trumpet and quaking mountain. Revelation repeats the formula at 4:5, 8:5, 11:19 and 16:18-21, adding an element each time (earthquake, then hail, then a great earthquake and huge hail), a deliberate crescendo that links the end of each sevenfold series.
symbols.cultural: Asia Minor was earthquake country: Sardis and Philadelphia were devastated in AD 17, and Laodicea in about AD 60.
symbols.meaning: A structural marker. Bauckham showed that the escalating storm formula ties the seventh seal, seventh trumpet and seventh bowl to the same climax, which many take as evidence that the three series end at the same point (recapitulation) rather than in simple sequence.

readings.reading: Evidence for recapitulation: each series ends in the final theophany.
Literal cosmic and seismic events, often read with a progressive (telescoping) structure in which each series grows out of the last.

symbols.phrase: First trumpet: hail and fire mixed with blood
symbols.jewish: The seventh Egyptian plague (Exodus 9:23-26) of hail with fire flashing through it, which struck plants and trees. Blood and fire together recall Joel 2:30-31 and Ezekiel 38:22 (fire, hail and bloodshed against Gog). Wisdom of Solomon 16:16-22 meditates on fire raging in hail as creation fighting for the righteous.
symbols.cultural: Burning of crops and orchards was a standard tactic of invading armies in the ancient world.
symbols.meaning: The first of four judgments on the created order, partial (a third) and patterned on the Exodus: God is again judging an oppressor so as to deliver his people. The note that "all the green grass" burns while 9:4 still mentions grass is often cited to show the visions are not a strictly literal chronicle.

readings.reading: The Gothic invasions under Alaric (c. 400-410), ending in the sack of Rome, a storm from the north on the western empire (Elliott, Barnes).
Devastation of the land of Israel as Roman armies burned crops and trees in the campaign of AD 67-70; Josephus records the stripping of trees around Jerusalem for siege works.
Literal ecological catastrophe in the future Tribulation, possibly by natural or military means.
Recurring natural disasters through history that warn humanity and limit its resources.

symbols.phrase: A third (of earth, trees, sea, waters, lights, mankind)
symbols.jewish: Ezekiel 5:2, 12 divides Jerusalem's people into thirds (burned, slain, scattered); Zechariah 13:8-9 has two thirds cut off and a third refined. The fraction thus belongs to prophetic judgment-and-remnant language.
symbols.meaning: A substantial but limited portion: the trumpets are severe yet not final, greater than the quarter of the fourth seal (6:8) and less than the totality of the bowls. The point is restraint that leaves room for repentance (9:20-21).

readings.reading: Often taken geopolitically as the third of the Roman world (the western empire, then the eastern), following the triple division of the empire.
Usually literal proportions of the earth affected.
A symbolic proportion marking partial, warning judgment.

symbols.phrase: Second trumpet: something like a great mountain burning, thrown into the sea
symbols.jewish: Jeremiah 51:25 calls Babylon a destroying mountain that God will make a burnt mountain; Jeremiah 51:42 says the sea will cover her. Jesus speaks of a mountain cast into the sea (Mark 11:23, spoken near the temple mount). 1 Enoch 18:13 and 21:3 describe disobedient stars as "great burning mountains", and Sibylline Oracles 5.158-161 has a great star fall into the sea and burn Babylon (Rome).
symbols.cultural: Vesuvius erupted in AD 79, destroying Pompeii and darkening the Bay of Naples; Pliny the Younger described the eruption. Sea trade was the lifeblood of Asian cities like Ephesus and Smyrna, so the loss of a third of ships threatened the economy that Revelation 18 later mourns.
symbols.meaning: A judgment on the sea and its commerce, echoing the first Egyptian plague (water to blood, Exodus 7:20-21). John says "something like" a mountain, signalling a vision rather than a description.

readings.reading: Chilton and others read the mountain as Jerusalem/Mount Zion, the apostate "mountain", cast into the sea of the nations (cf. Mark 11:23); some note the Jewish fleet destroyed at Joppa and the sea of Galilee battle in Josephus (Jewish War 3.9.3; 3.10.9).
Genseric's Vandals, a naval power that ravaged Mediterranean islands and coasts and sacked Rome by sea in 455 (Elliott, Barnes).
Possibly a literal meteor, asteroid or volcanic mass striking the ocean in the Tribulation.
God's judgment on the commercial and maritime structures humans trust, recurring in every age; some see allusion to Babylon's fall (Jeremiah 51).

symbols.phrase: Third trumpet: a great star named Wormwood
symbols.jewish: Wormwood (Artemisia, a bitter plant) is a prophetic image of the bitterness of judgment and apostasy: God will make idolatrous Israel drink wormwood and poisoned water (Jeremiah 9:15; 23:15); Deuteronomy 29:18 warns of a root bearing poison and wormwood among those who turn to other gods; Amos 5:7 and 6:12 speak of justice turned to wormwood. A fallen star recalls Isaiah 14:12 (the king of Babylon as a fallen morning star) and the fallen watchers of 1 Enoch 86-88. The scene reverses the sweetening of Marah's bitter water (Exodus 15:23-25).
symbols.cultural: Wormwood was used in antiquity as a medicine and vermifuge and was known to be bitter but not usually lethal, which underlines the symbolic character of the deaths. Popular modern claims that "Chernobyl" means wormwood are inexact (the name refers to mugwort, a related Artemisia) and are not part of scholarly exegesis.
symbols.meaning: Judgment on fresh water, the source of life, under a name that recalls the punishment of idolatry. The star is probably an agent of judgment (angelic or symbolic) rather than an astronomical body only.

readings.reading: Attila the Hun, "the scourge of God", whose campaigns (c. 440-453) swept the river regions of the Danube, Rhine and Po (Elliott, Barnes).

Apostate Israel itself, or its leadership, fallen from heaven and turning the land's waters bitter, echoing Jeremiah 9:15; Chilton connects it to Deuteronomy 29:18. Josephus describes the Jordan and Galilee choked with corpses in AD 67-68.
A literal celestial body (perhaps a comet or meteor) contaminating water supplies, or a powerful fallen angel.
Recurring judgments by which God lets idolaters taste the bitterness of their idolatry; the false teaching that poisons life.

symbols.phrase: Fourth trumpet: a third of the sun, moon and stars struck
symbols.jewish: The ninth Egyptian plague of darkness (Exodus 10:21-23). Prophetic texts use darkened luminaries for the fall of nations and the Day of the Lord (Isaiah 13:10 of Babylon; Ezekiel 32:7-8 of Egypt; Joel 2:10, 31; Amos 8:9). Jesus uses the same idiom in the Olivet Discourse (Matthew 24:29).
symbols.cultural: Eclipses and astral signs were read in the Roman world as omens of the fall of rulers; Roman writers (Suetonius, Tacitus) record portents around the deaths of emperors.
symbols.meaning: Darkness is the undoing of the creation of light (Genesis 1:14-18) and a classic sign of political and cosmic upheaval. Interpreters disagree whether the language is primarily literal or the conventional prophetic idiom for the collapse of powers.

readings.reading: The extinction of the western Roman emperorship (Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus in 476) and the eclipse of Rome's consuls and senate, the "lights" of the western third.
De-creation language for the collapse of Israel's political and religious order in AD 70, as in Isaiah 13 for Babylon.
Literal reduction of sunlight and moonlight during the Tribulation.
God's judgment on idolatrous society experienced as darkness and despair, recurring until the end.

symbols.phrase: An eagle flying in mid-heaven crying "Woe, woe, woe"
symbols.jewish: Hosea 8:1 sets the trumpet to the mouth because an eagle is over the Lord's house; Deuteronomy 28:49 threatens a nation swooping like an eagle against covenant-breakers; Habakkuk 1:8 likens the Babylonians to eagles. In 2 Baruch 77:17-26 an eagle carries Baruch's letter to the exiles, and in 4 Ezra 11-12 the eagle is Rome. Some later manuscripts (followed by the KJV) read "angel" instead of "eagle"; the earliest witnesses read "eagle". "Woe" is the prophetic lament-oracle (Isaiah 5; Amos 5:18).
symbols.cultural: The eagle (aquila) was the sacred standard of every Roman legion and an emblem of Jupiter; a heavenly eagle announcing doom would strike readers who knew the legions' standards.
symbols.meaning: A herald (perhaps one of the four living creatures, the third of which is like an eagle, Revelation 4:7) announcing that the last three trumpets are worse and are directed at "those who dwell on the earth", Revelation's phrase for unbelieving humanity hostile to God's people (6:10; 13:8).

readings.reading: Recalls Deuteronomy 28:49 and Hosea 8:1: the covenant curse of an eagle-like (Roman) army falling on Israel; some note the legionary eagles set up in the temple courts in AD 70 (Josephus, Jewish War 6.6.1).
The three woes are the Saracen, Turkish and final (often papal or French Revolution era) woe trumpets.
A literal heavenly messenger warning the world in the Tribulation.

symbols.phrase: Those who dwell on the earth
symbols.jewish: The phrase echoes Isaiah 24:1-6 and 26:9, 21 (judgment on the earth's inhabitants). In 1 Enoch (e.g. 37:5; 54:9) "those who dwell on the earth" can denote the wicked who are judged, and in Hebrew "the land" (ha-aretz) can mean the land of Israel.
symbols.meaning: In Revelation the phrase consistently names unbelievers who persecute the saints and worship the beast (6:10; 11:10; 13:8, 12, 14; 17:2, 8). The dispute is over scope.

readings.reading: Translates as "those who dwell on the land", that is, the inhabitants of Judea and Jerusalem under covenant judgment (Gentry, Chilton).
The unbelieving population of the whole world during the Tribulation.
Humanity whose home and loyalties are in this present order rather than in God.

The trumpets are the covenant curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 falling on Judea and Jerusalem in the Jewish War (AD 66-70). The fire from the altar recalls Ezekiel 10 and the burning of Jerusalem; the burning mountain cast into the sea is Mount Zion's fall; Wormwood is apostate Israel (Jeremiah 9:15); "those who dwell on the land" are the people of Judea. Chilton and Gentry stress the Jericho pattern: seven trumpets announce the fall of the city that rejected God's messengers. This reading depends on a pre-70 date of Revelation, which is disputed.

The seventh seal opens a new era of judgments on the Roman Empire after its Christianisation. The four trumpets fall on the western third of the empire: Alaric's Goths (first), Genseric's Vandals by sea (second), Attila's Huns along the rivers (third), and the extinction of the western emperor in 476 (fourth), as set out in detail by Elliott's Horae Apocalypticae and Barnes's Notes. The eagle's three woes introduce the Saracens, the Turks and the final judgments.

The trumpets are literal, future judgments in the seven-year Tribulation that follow and intensify the seal judgments, unfolding out of the seventh seal (Walvoord, Thomas). They involve real ecological and astronomical catastrophes on a third of the world; the eagle (or angel) gives a final warning before the demonic woe judgments of chapter 9.

The trumpets recapitulate the period between Christ's ascension and return from the angle of warning. Like the Exodus plagues they show God judging an idolatrous world through disasters in nature and society, partially (a third), so that people might repent, while answering the prayers of the persecuted church (Hendriksen, Beale in modified form). The final trumpet, like the final seal and bowl, brings the last judgment.

Many recent commentators (Beale, Osborne, Koester, Keener) combine approaches: the imagery is drawn from the Exodus and prophetic judgment oracles and spoke to first-century Asia (sea trade, Roman power), it describes recurring patterns of judgment through the church age, and it climaxes in the still-future consummation. They typically see the series as overlapping rather than strictly sequential.

Like partial preterists, full preterists place all the trumpets in the period ending in AD 70, but they also identify the seventh trumpet of this series with the "last trumpet" of 1 Corinthians 15 and the resurrection, held to have been fulfilled spiritually then. This conclusion places full preterism outside the historic creeds, which confess a future bodily resurrection; proponents reply that Scripture, not the creeds, must govern.

questions: What does it mean that the trumpet judgments are presented as God's answer to the prayers of the saints (Revelation 8:3-5)? How should that shape the way Christians pray about injustice?
Trace the parallels between the first four trumpets and the plagues of Egypt. What does the Exodus pattern suggest about whom the judgments are against and whom they are for?
Why does the text keep limiting the judgments to "a third"? How do the different views explain this restraint?

Does the seventh seal contain the trumpets, or do the seals, trumpets and bowls describe the same period from different angles? What evidence (such as the repeated thunder-earthquake formula) bears on the question?

title: The fifth and sixth trumpets: locusts from the Abyss and the cavalry from the Euphrates
summary: The fifth trumpet (the first woe) shows a star fallen from heaven that receives the key to the Abyss; smoke pours out, and from it come locust-like creatures with scorpion stings that torment, but may not kill, those without God's seal for five months. Their king is the angel of the Abyss, Abaddon or Apollyon, "Destroyer". The sixth trumpet (the second woe) releases four angels bound at the Euphrates, and a cavalry of two hundred million, with lion-headed horses breathing fire, smoke and sulfur, kills a third of humanity. Yet the survivors do not repent of idolatry, murder, sorcery, sexual immorality or theft, which shows that the trumpets aim at repentance and that judgment alone does not produce it.

outline.heading: Fifth trumpet: the fallen star opens the Abyss
Locusts that torment the unsealed for five months
Description of the locusts and their king Abaddon/Apollyon
The first woe passes
Sixth trumpet: the four angels at the Euphrates released
The two hundred million cavalry
The rest of humanity does not repent

context:
The fifth trumpet expands the eighth Egyptian plague (Exodus 10:12-20) through Joel 1-2, where a locust swarm is described as an invading army with teeth like lions and the appearance of horses, the herald of the Day of the Lord. Locust plagues were a real terror in the ancient Near East and appear among the covenant curses (Deuteronomy 28:38, 42). The Abyss draws on Second Temple traditions about rebellious angels imprisoned until the judgment (1 Enoch 10:4-6, 18-21, 88; Jubilees 5:6-10; Luke 8:31; 2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6), so the scene is widely read as a demonic plague released under God's permission and limited by his seal. Abaddon ("destruction") is a poetic name for the realm of the dead in Job, Psalms and Proverbs and is personified in the Qumran Thanksgiving Hymns.

The sixth trumpet turns east. The Euphrates was the ideal border of the land promised to Abraham (Genesis 15:18) and the river beyond which Israel's invaders, Assyria and Babylon, came (Isaiah 8:7; Jeremiah 46:10). In the first century it was Rome's frontier with Parthia, whose mounted archers had destroyed Crassus's army at Carrhae (53 BC) and humiliated a Roman force at Rhandeia (AD 62). Parthian horsemen were famed for long hair and for shooting arrows backwards while riding away (the "Parthian shot"), which many see behind the creatures whose power is in their tails. The legend that Nero would return from the east with Parthian armies (Sibylline Oracles 4.119-139; 5.361-368; Tacitus, Histories 2.8) and 1 Enoch 56:5-8, where angels stir up the Parthians and Medes against the land, show how charged the Euphrates image was. The vice list in 9:20-21 reflects Jewish polemic against idols that cannot see, hear or walk (Psalm 115:4-7; Daniel 5:23; Wisdom of Solomon 13-15) and the trade-guild idolatry pressed on Christians in Asia.

symbols.phrase: A star fallen from heaven given the key to the shaft of the Abyss
symbols.jewish: Stars represent angels in Jewish apocalyptic (Judges 5:20; Job 38:7; Daniel 8:10; Revelation 1:20). 1 Enoch 86-88 portrays the fallen watchers as stars that fall from heaven and are bound in the abyss; Isaiah 14:12 depicts the king of Babylon as a fallen star. Keys signify delegated authority (Isaiah 22:22); in Revelation 1:18 Christ holds the keys of death and Hades and in 20:1 an angel holds the key of the Abyss.
symbols.meaning: An angelic agent. The perfect tense "had fallen" leads many to see a fallen angel, perhaps Satan (cf. Luke 10:18; Revelation 12:9), though others hold it is simply a good angel descending, as in 20:1. Either way, the key is "given": evil acts only within limits set by God.

readings.reading: Often identified with Muhammad (Barnes, Elliott), or with the apostate influences that opened the way to Islam in the seventh century.
Usually Satan or a fallen angel, literally releasing demonic hordes in the Tribulation (Walvoord).
Satan or a fallen angel, permitted throughout the age to unleash spiritual deception and torment on unbelievers.

Satan or a fallen angel unleashing demonic oppression on apostate Israel during the war years; Chilton links it to Jesus' warning of the unclean spirit returning sevenfold to "this evil generation" (Matthew 12:43-45).

symbols.phrase: The pit of the Abyss
symbols.jewish: The Greek abyssos renders the Hebrew tehom, the primeval deep of Genesis 1:2 and Psalm 107:26, and came to mean the underworld prison of evil spirits: 1 Enoch 10:4-6, 13 and 18:11-16 (a chasm of fire where disobedient stars are bound), 21:7-10, Jubilees 5:6-10. Demons beg Jesus not to send them into the Abyss (Luke 8:31). Romans 10:7 uses it for the realm of the dead.
symbols.cultural: Greek mythology had a parallel in Tartarus, the deep prison of the Titans (2 Peter 2:4 uses the verb "tartarize").
symbols.meaning: The source of demonic evil and later of the beast (11:7; 17:8) and the place where Satan is bound (20:1-3). Its opening means God permits a measured outbreak of demonic power as judgment.

symbols.phrase: Smoke like the smoke of a great furnace, darkening sun and air
symbols.jewish: Smoke from a furnace rose from Sodom and Gomorrah after their destruction (Genesis 19:28) and from Sinai at God's descent (Exodus 19:18). Locust swarms dense enough to darken the land are described in Exodus 10:15 and Joel 2:10.
symbols.meaning: An image of judgment and spiritual darkness; the darkening may also anticipate the swarm itself, since huge locust clouds literally blot out the sun.

readings.reading: The spread of Islam and its doctrine, which historicists described as darkening the "sun" of the gospel in the East.
Deception and spiritual blindness released on those who reject God.

symbols.phrase: Locusts with power like scorpions
symbols.jewish: The eighth Egyptian plague (Exodus 10:4-15) and the locust army of Joel 1-2, a figure for invading nations and the Day of the Lord. Locusts are among the covenant curses for disobedience (Deuteronomy 28:38, 42; 1 Kings 8:37). Scorpions symbolise hostile, painful forces (Ezekiel 2:6; Deuteronomy 8:15; Luke 10:19, where Jesus gives disciples authority over serpents and scorpions). Wisdom of Solomon 16:9 recalls the Egyptians killed by the bites of locusts and flies.
symbols.cultural: Locust plagues periodically devastated Syria, Palestine and Asia Minor. Scorpions were common in the region, and their sting causes intense pain but is rarely fatal to adults, which fits the limit "torment, not kill". The locust was associated with Apollo, honoured in some places as a locust-averting god (Apollo Parnopios).
symbols.meaning: A hybrid plague of demonic torment: real locusts eat vegetation, but these are forbidden to touch plants and attack only people, so the image is not of an ordinary insect swarm.

readings.reading: The Saracen (Arab Muslim) armies of the seventh and eighth centuries, coming from Arabia, the land of locust swarms; the order not to hurt grass was compared to Abu Bakr's reported instruction not to destroy palm trees or crops (Barnes, Elliott).
A demonic plague of madness and torment on Judea in the war years, or the Roman siege forces; Chilton stresses demonic oppression and the internal Zealot terror described by Josephus.
Literal demonic beings released in the Tribulation (Walvoord, Thomas); popular writers (e.g. Hal Lindsey) once suggested attack helicopters, a reading most futurist scholars do not adopt.
Demonic forces that torment unbelievers with the inner misery, fear and emptiness of life without God, throughout history (Hendriksen).

symbols.phrase: Only those without the seal of God on their foreheads harmed
keywords: seal of god on their foreheads
symbols.jewish: Ezekiel 9:4-6 has a mark (the Hebrew letter tav) put on the foreheads of those who grieve over Jerusalem's abominations, so that they are spared the slaughter. In the Exodus plagues Israel in Goshen was spared (Exodus 8:22; 9:4, 26) and the blood on the doorposts protected the firstborn (Exodus 12:13). Psalms of Solomon 15:6-9 speaks of the mark of God on the righteous for salvation.
symbols.cultural: Slaves and soldiers in the Roman world could be branded or tattooed to show ownership; seals on documents and goods marked owners' protection.
symbols.meaning: Refers back to the sealing of the servants of God in 7:3-8. Believers are protected from this spiritual plague (not necessarily from physical suffering or martyrdom, which Revelation expects), while the plague falls on those who bear no mark of belonging to God.

readings.reading: Includes the literal 144,000 Jewish servants sealed in chapter 7, and other believers living in the Tribulation.
All true believers, sealed by the Spirit (Ephesians 1:13), preserved from demonic deception.
The Christian remnant in Judea who heeded Jesus' warning and fled before the siege (Luke 21:20-21; Eusebius, Church History 3.5 on flight to Pella).

symbols.phrase: Tormented for five months
symbols.jewish: The lifespan of a locust is about five months, roughly the dry season from spring to late summer. The floodwaters prevailed for 150 days (Genesis 7:24; 8:3). Some see a limited, divinely set period of judgment.
symbols.cultural: Locust swarms in the eastern Mediterranean typically appear in spring and summer.
symbols.meaning: A limited, relatively short period of torment, framed by the natural locust season. Interpreters differ on whether it is a literal span or symbolic of a restricted period.

readings.reading: Using the day-for-a-year principle, 150 years of Saracen expansion, often dated from c. 612 (the start of Muhammad's preaching) to 762 (the founding of Baghdad, when the caliphate settled), or similar ranges (Elliott, Barnes).

A literal five-month period in the war, often linked to the five months of Gessius Florus's outrages in AD 66 (May to September) or to the five-month siege of Jerusalem in AD 70 (roughly April to September).
A literal five months within the Tribulation.
A symbolic, limited time: the torment is real but restrained.

symbols.phrase: People will seek death and not find it
symbols.jewish: Job 3:21 speaks of those who long for death that does not come; Jeremiah 8:3 says the survivors of judgment will prefer death to life. Hosea 10:8 and Revelation 6:16 have people calling on mountains to cover them.
symbols.cultural: Suicide was regarded by Stoics as an honourable exit; denying even that escape intensifies the horror.
symbols.meaning: The torment is psychological and spiritual as much as physical: life becomes unbearable, yet no escape is granted. It portrays the despair of life under judgment without repentance.

symbols.phrase: Horses prepared for battle, crowns of gold, human faces, women's hair, lions' teeth, iron breastplates
symbols.jewish: Joel 2:4-5 says the locusts look like horses and sound like chariots; Joel 1:6 gives them teeth like a lion's. The resemblance of a locust's head to a horse's head was noticed in antiquity (Italian cavalletta and German Heupferd, "hay-horse", preserve it). The sound of chariots rushing into battle echoes Joel 2:5. Crowns suggest authority to conquer, as with the first rider in Revelation 6:2.
symbols.cultural: Parthian cavalry were known for long, flowing hair; armoured cavalry (cataphracts) wore scale or iron breastplates. Locusts' antennae could be likened to hair, and their thorax plates to armour.
symbols.meaning: A nightmarish composite that turns Joel's locust army into an invincible, intelligent, cruel host: human faces suggest intelligence, women's hair perhaps seduction or wildness, lions' teeth ferocity, and iron breastplates invulnerability. The piling up of "like" shows John is describing a visionary image, not a zoological species.

readings.reading: Detailed matches with Arab warriors: turbans like crowns, beards (faces of men), long hair, mounted on horses, armour, as argued by Barnes and Elliott.
A description of grotesque demonic beings, perhaps visible, in the Tribulation.
Either demonic forces or the Roman and Zealot armies, depicted with Joel's locust-army imagery to show the Day of the Lord against Jerusalem.
Symbolic portrait of the power, cunning and cruelty of demonic forces.

symbols.phrase: Their king, the angel of the Abyss: Abaddon in Hebrew, Apollyon in Greek
symbols.jewish: Abaddon ("destruction", "place of destruction") is a poetic parallel to Sheol and death (Job 26:6; 28:22; 31:12; Psalm 88:11; Proverbs 15:11; 27:20). In the Qumran Thanksgiving Hymns (1QH 11:16-19) the torrents of Belial burst into Abaddon, a step toward personifying it. Proverbs 30:27 observes that locusts have no king, so a king over these locusts marks them as unnatural.
symbols.cultural: Apollyon ("Destroyer") is probably a pun on Apollo, whose name some ancient writers derived from the verb "to destroy" (apollumi) and whose symbols included the locust. Emperors associated themselves with Apollo, notably Nero (who performed as Apollo the lyre-player) and Augustus; Domitian was also linked to him. Many scholars therefore see a jab at the imperial claim: the god the emperors honour is the destroyer from the pit. The pun is widely accepted but not certain.
symbols.meaning: The ruler of the demonic locusts, the personification of destruction. Some identify him with Satan, others with a subordinate demon or with the fallen star of 9:1. The bilingual name presents a hellish counterpart to the Lamb who rules.

readings.reading: Variously the Saracen caliph or Muhammad as the leader of the destructive armies (Barnes notes the destructive character of the Muslim conquests).
A specific powerful demon or Satan himself, leading literal demonic forces in the future.
Satan as destroyer, with a possible allusion to Nero, the Apollo-imitating emperor of the war years.
Satan or a chief demon whose work in every age is destruction, in contrast to Christ who gives life.

symbols.phrase: The first woe has passed; two woes still to come
symbols.jewish: Woe-oracles were a standard prophetic form (Isaiah 5:8-22; Habakkuk 2:6-19). The triad of woes echoes the eagle's cry in 8:13.
symbols.meaning: A structural marker: the fifth, sixth and seventh trumpets are the three woes. The third woe is announced (11:14) but not explicitly labelled; many locate it in the seventh trumpet and its outworking (chapters 12-16, including the devil's descent in 12:12).

symbols.phrase: A voice from the four horns of the golden altar before God
keywords: four horns of the golden altar
symbols.jewish: The golden altar of incense had four horns (Exodus 30:1-3, 10), on which the high priest put blood annually on the Day of Atonement. Horns of the altar were a place of asylum (1 Kings 1:50; 2:28), and their being cut off meant judgment (Amos 3:14). The voice links back to 8:3-5 and the martyrs' prayers.
symbols.meaning: The sixth trumpet is again presented as an answer to the prayers offered on the incense altar; the place of intercession and atonement becomes the source of the command to judge.

symbols.phrase: Four angels bound at the great river Euphrates
symbols.jewish: The Euphrates is the northern boundary of the promised land (Genesis 15:18; Deuteronomy 1:7; Joshua 1:4), the river from which Assyria and Babylon came as God's instruments of judgment (Isaiah 7:20; 8:7-8; Jeremiah 46:10; Jeremiah 13:4-7). 1 Enoch 56:5-8 predicts that angels will stir up the Parthians and Medes to invade the land of the elect. Bound angels recall 1 Enoch 10:4-12 and Jubilees 5:6. The "four" may relate to the four winds (Revelation 7:1).
symbols.cultural: In John's day the Euphrates was Rome's eastern frontier and the border with the Parthian empire, Rome's most feared rival; the Parthians had defeated Crassus at Carrhae (53 BC) and forced a Roman army to surrender at Rhandeia (AD 62). The Nero redivivus legend expected Nero to return leading Parthian hosts against Rome (Sibylline Oracles 4.119-139).
symbols.meaning: Evil angels held in check until a precise time ordained by God now unleash a massive invasion from the east, the classic direction of Israel's judgment. The "hour, day, month and year" stresses divine timing: nothing happens before God's appointed moment.

readings.reading: The four Turkish sultanates (Seljuk powers) settled near the Euphrates, released to overthrow the eastern Roman empire; the hour, day, month and year was computed as about 391 years (and 15 days) from roughly 1057 to the fall of Constantinople in 1453 (Elliott, Barnes). Josiah Litch (1838) famously applied a related calculation to predict the fall of Ottoman power in August 1840.

Roman legions massed in the Euphrates region and Syria (Josephus notes troops drawn from the Euphrates garrison for Titus's siege, Jewish War 5.1.6), loosed upon Judea; the Euphrates recalls Babylon's invasion of 587 BC.
A literal future invasion from the east, often linked to the kings of the east of Revelation 16:12, perhaps involving Asian powers, or a demonic army (Walvoord).
The river stands for the boundary from which threatening, destructive powers come; demonic forces stirring warfare across history.

symbols.phrase: Mounted troops numbering two hundred million
symbols.jewish: The Greek is literally "two myriads of myriads", an expression for an incalculable number; compare the thousands and myriads of Daniel 7:10 and the vast chariots of God in Psalm 68:17. Ancient armies numbered in the tens of thousands; the whole Roman army was perhaps 300,000.
symbols.cultural: Parthian armies were famous for their mounted archers, and the idea of countless eastern cavalry was a Roman nightmare.
symbols.meaning: An overwhelming, unimaginable army. Most interpreters read the figure as hyperbolic and symbolic (an innumerable host) rather than as a literal census; John hears the number, stressing its revelatory not observational character.

readings.reading: Some futurists take the number literally, noting that modern populations make an army of this size conceivable (some popular writers pointed to China); others, including Walvoord, allow that the hosts may be demonic.
The vast Turkish cavalry hosts that overran Asia Minor and the Balkans.
The overwhelming Roman forces and auxiliaries arrayed against Jerusalem, described with exaggerated numbering typical of apocalyptic.
Symbol of demonic forces numberless in their reach, warring against humanity across the ages.

symbols.phrase: Breastplates of fire, hyacinth and sulfur; lion-headed horses breathing fire, smoke and sulfur
symbols.jewish: Fire and sulfur (brimstone) rained on Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24, 28), and fire with brimstone is the punishment of Gog (Ezekiel 38:22) and of the wicked (Psalm 11:6; Isaiah 34:9). The leviathan breathes fire and smoke (Job 41:19-21). Lions' heads recall Joel's lion-toothed locusts and suggest royal ferocity. The colours (fiery red, dark blue hyacinth, sulfurous yellow) match the three plagues.
symbols.cultural: The Greek "hyakinthinos" (BSB "sapphire") denotes a dark blue-violet, the colour of the smoke from burning sulfur. Fire-breathing hybrid monsters such as the Chimaera (lion-headed, serpent-tailed) were familiar from Greek myth and art in Asia Minor (Lycia).
symbols.meaning: The riders and horses are infernal: they bear the colours and weapons of hell itself. The three plagues of fire, smoke and sulfur anticipate the lake of fire and sulfur (Revelation 19:20; 21:8).

readings.reading: Barnes and Elliott saw here a description of Turkish cavalry with gunpowder and cannon, which the Ottomans used decisively in the siege of Constantinople in 1453: fire and smoke and sulfur issuing from the "mouths" of guns.
Either literal demonic creatures or, in some popular readings, modern weaponry; Walvoord leaves open demonic hosts.
Hellish, destructive warfare described with the imagery of Sodom's judgment.

symbols.phrase: Power in their mouths and in their tails like serpents with heads
symbols.jewish: Serpents bring God's judgment in Numbers 21:6 and Jeremiah 8:17, and recall the serpent of Genesis 3; Isaiah 9:15 says the prophet who teaches lies is the "tail". The scorpion-tailed locusts of 9:10 are matched here by serpent-tailed horses.
symbols.cultural: The Parthian cavalry tactic of feigned retreat while shooting arrows backward over the horse's rump made their "tails" dangerous; Roman writers (e.g. Plutarch on Crassus) describe it. Lion-headed, serpent-tailed beasts like the Chimaera were standard monsters in Greek art.
symbols.meaning: The creatures harm both coming and going, a picture of inescapable, demonic destruction. The serpent link ties the plague to the dragon, "that ancient serpent" (12:9).

readings.reading: Barnes linked the tails to the horse-tail standards (tughs) used as Turkish insignia of rank by pashas.
An allusion to eastern (Parthian-style) cavalry tactics among the forces that ravaged Judea.

symbols.phrase: The rest did not repent of idols, murder, sorcery, immorality and theft
symbols.jewish: The polemic against idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone and wood that cannot see, hear or walk comes from Psalm 115:4-7, Psalm 135:15-17 and Daniel 5:4, 23, and Deuteronomy 32:17 identifies idol-worship with demon-worship (also 1 Corinthians 10:20). Wisdom of Solomon 14:22-27 traces murder, theft and sexual corruption to idolatry. The hardening echoes Pharaoh's refusal to let Israel go despite the plagues (Exodus 7-11). The vice list echoes the Decalogue's second table.
symbols.cultural: In the cities of Asia, idols stood in temples, homes and guild halls; trade guilds held banquets in honour of patron gods, and refusal to participate cost Christians economically (compare Revelation 2:14, 20). "Sorcery" (pharmakeia) covers magic and drug-related spells, flourishing in Ephesus (Acts 19:19).
symbols.meaning: The goal of the trumpet judgments is repentance, but judgments alone do not soften hearts; the gospel witness of chapters 10-11 is the next step. The verses show the moral roots of judgment: false worship produces social evil.

readings.reading: The unreformed Christendom of the Middle Ages, whose saint-and-image veneration historicist Protestants called idolatry, did not repent despite the Saracen and Turkish scourges; the next vision (ch. 10) is the Reformation.
Applied by some to the pagan world and to apostate Judaism which, as the war progressed, did not turn; others stress that the idolatry language suits Gentile Asia and the world beyond Judea.
Shows the hardness of humanity in the Tribulation, setting up the final bowl judgments.
A permanent truth about fallen humanity: suffering alone does not convert.

The fifth and sixth trumpets describe the escalating horrors of the Jewish War. The locusts are a demonic plague of torment and madness unleashed on the land, which Chilton relates to Jesus' saying that the unclean spirit would return with seven others to "this evil generation" (Matthew 12:43-45) and to the factional terror inside Jerusalem described by Josephus; the five months may be the summer of AD 66 or the siege of AD 70. The Euphrates armies are the Roman legions gathered from the east under Vespasian and Titus. The failure to repent is the failure of the generation that rejected the Messiah. This depends on a pre-70 date for Revelation, which most scholars dispute.

The fifth trumpet is the rise of Islam and the Saracen conquests from Arabia (the fallen star often identified with Muhammad); the five months are 150 years by the year-day principle. The sixth trumpet is the Turkish (Seljuk and Ottoman) power released from the Euphrates, whose fixed period of about 391 years ends with the fall of Constantinople in 1453, taken with gunpowder and cannon (the fire, smoke and sulfur). The unrepentant are western Christendom, still given to image-veneration, which sets the stage for the Reformation in chapter 10 (Elliott, Barnes).

These are literal future judgments in the second half of the Tribulation. The locusts are demonic beings released from the Abyss who torment unbelievers for five literal months; the two hundred million are a massive army (some take it literally as a human force from the east, others as demonic cavalry) that kills a third of the world's population. Humanity's refusal to repent demonstrates the justice of the final bowls (Walvoord, Thomas).

The locusts portray the demonic torment, inner emptiness and despair experienced by those who reject God throughout the church age, while believers sealed by the Spirit are protected. The Euphrates army represents the destructive warfare, often demonically driven, that recurs across history, culminating before the end. The unrepentant response shows that judgment cannot by itself transform hearts (Hendriksen, Beale).

Commentators such as Beale, Osborne and Koester see the locusts as demonic agents (following Enochic traditions about the Abyss), the Euphrates cavalry as evoking first-century fear of Parthian invasion, and the whole as both a pattern of judgment during the church age and a foreshadowing of an intensified final outbreak before Christ's return. They generally hold that the images are not meant to be decoded into specific historical events.

questions: Why might John describe the locusts with so many conflicting features (horse, human face, women's hair, lion teeth, scorpion tail)? What does that suggest about how to read the vision?
How does the seal of God in Revelation 9:4 relate to the sealing in Revelation 7? What kind of protection is promised to believers?
What associations would the Euphrates have had for a Jewish reader and for a Roman reader in Asia? How do those associations shape the different views?
Revelation 9:20-21 says that the survivors did not repent. What does this teach about the relationship between suffering, judgment and repentance?
Historicists have computed precise dates from "the hour, day, month and year". What are the strengths and dangers of such calculations?

title: The mighty angel and the little scroll
section: The seven trumpets: interlude before the seventh trumpet (Revelation 10:1-11:14)
summary: Between the sixth and seventh trumpets, as between the sixth and seventh seals, comes an interlude. A mighty angel, clothed with a cloud, crowned with a rainbow, with a face like the sun and legs like pillars of fire, plants one foot on the sea and one on the land, holding a small open scroll. He roars like a lion and seven thunders speak, but John is told to seal up what they said. The angel swears by the Creator that there will be no more delay: when the seventh trumpet sounds, the mystery of God announced to the prophets will be fulfilled. John, like Ezekiel, is told to eat the scroll, sweet in his mouth and bitter in his stomach, and is recommissioned to prophesy again about many peoples, nations, languages and kings.

outline.heading: The mighty angel with the open little scroll
The seven thunders sealed up
The oath: no more delay; the mystery of God to be fulfilled
John eats the scroll: sweet and bitter
John recommissioned to prophesy again

context:
Chapter 10 is a prophetic call narrative modelled on Ezekiel 2:8-3:3, where the prophet is given a scroll written with lament and woe, eats it and finds it sweet as honey, and is then sent to a rebellious house. The oath of the angel with raised hand comes from Daniel 12:7, where a man clothed in linen above the river swears by the one who lives forever that the end will come after "a time, times and half a time", the very period that chapter 11 takes up (42 months, 1,260 days). Daniel was told to seal up his words until the end (Daniel 12:4, 9); John is told to seal up only the seven thunders, while the rest of his prophecy is to be left open (Revelation 22:10), a signal that the end-time revelation Daniel awaited has begun. The "mystery" fulfilled echoes Daniel 2 and Amos 3:7; at Qumran the Habakkuk Pesher (1QpHab 7:1-5) says God made known to the Teacher of Righteousness all the mysteries of the prophets, though their final fulfilment was being prolonged.

For Asian readers, a colossal figure astride sea and land would recall the Colossus of Rhodes, the giant bronze statue of the sun-god Helios (fallen in an earthquake c. 226 BC but still a famous wonder), and the radiant sun-crown that emperors such as Nero adopted on coins. The scene asserts that true cosmic sovereignty belongs to the Creator. Structurally, the interlude explains how the church's prophetic witness fits into the judgments: the trumpets have not produced repentance (9:20-21), so the next movement turns to the witnessing church (11:1-13). Many scholars (Bauckham, Beale) argue that the little scroll is the same scroll the Lamb opened in chapter 5, now given to John to prophesy; others distinguish them.

symbols.phrase: Another mighty angel coming down from heaven
symbols.jewish: The figure combines features of the man clothed in linen of Daniel 10:5-6 and 12:6-7 and of God's glory in Ezekiel 1:26-28. The earlier "mighty angel" of Revelation 5:2 asked who was worthy to open the scroll, and a third appears in 18:21. Some find a wordplay on Gabriel ("God is mighty"), who interprets Daniel's visions.
symbols.cultural: The image of a giant astride land and sea evokes the Colossus of Rhodes, a famous statue of Helios standing at the harbour of Rhodes, off the coast of Asia.
symbols.meaning: A powerful angelic messenger reflecting divine glory. Whether he is Christ is disputed: his features (cloud, rainbow, sun-like face, fiery legs) recall the description of Christ in 1:13-16 and of God in 4:3, but Revelation never calls Christ an angel, and the angel swears by God rather than as God.

readings.reading: Many historicists (Elliott, Barnes) see Christ himself, or Christ's coming in the Reformation, with the angel's descent representing the renewed light of the gospel in the sixteenth century.
Chilton takes the angel as Christ, the covenant Lord who comes to announce judgment and to commission the church's witness against Israel.
Most dispensational futurists (Walvoord, Thomas) treat him as a strong created angel, not Christ.
Beale argues the angel is the Angel of the Lord, a manifestation of Christ; Hendriksen also sees Christ; others in the idealist tradition think a high angel.

symbols.phrase: Wrapped in a cloud, a rainbow over his head, face like the sun, legs like pillars of fire
symbols.jewish: Clouds are the vehicle of theophany and of the Son of Man (Exodus 19:9; Daniel 7:13; Psalm 104:3). The rainbow surrounds God's throne in Ezekiel 1:28 and Revelation 4:3 and recalls the covenant mercy after the flood (Genesis 9:13-16). The sun-like face recalls Moses after Sinai (Exodus 34:29-35), the transfiguration (Matthew 17:2) and Christ in Revelation 1:16. The pillars of fire and cloud guided Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 13:21-22).
symbols.cultural: Sun-rays and radiant crowns were symbols of Helios and Sol, and emperors (Nero, later Domitian) appeared with radiate crowns on coins. Here such glory belongs to God's messenger.
symbols.meaning: The angel bears the attributes of God's presence: judgment (cloud and fire), mercy (rainbow) and glory (sun). The wilderness imagery suggests a new Exodus, guiding God's people through judgment, and the rainbow suggests that judgment is tempered by covenant faithfulness.

symbols.phrase: A small scroll lying open in his hand
symbols.jewish: Ezekiel receives a scroll written on both sides with lament, mourning and woe (Ezekiel 2:9-10). Daniel's words were sealed until the end (Daniel 12:4, 9). Zechariah 5:1-4 sees a flying scroll of curse. The Lamb took the sealed scroll from God's hand in Revelation 5:1-7.
symbols.cultural: Scrolls (biblion, here the diminutive biblaridion) were the form of books and legal documents; an "open" scroll signifies a document whose seals have been broken and whose contents are in force.
symbols.meaning: The content John must now proclaim. Many scholars (Bauckham, Beale, Koester) identify it with the seven-sealed scroll of chapter 5, now opened by the Lamb and handed via the angel to John, so that the "little" description is relative to the giant angel. Others (Aune, many futurists) see a distinct, smaller message, often the contents of 11:1-13 or of chapters 11-22. The open scroll suggests God's plan now being revealed and carried out.

readings.reading: The Bible opened to the people at the Reformation, through printing and vernacular translation (Elliott, Barnes).
The message of judgment against Jerusalem and of the new covenant, which John must proclaim; Chilton sees it as the "new covenant" document given to the prophet.
A distinct scroll containing the prophecy of the remaining Tribulation events (often chapters 11-19).
The gospel and God's redemptive plan entrusted to the church, the same scroll as chapter 5 (Beale).

symbols.phrase: Right foot on the sea, left foot on the land
symbols.jewish: God made the sea and the dry land (Psalm 95:5; Jonah 1:9). Setting the foot on territory is a gesture of claiming possession (Joshua 1:3; 10:24; Psalm 8:6). In Revelation, the beast later rises from the sea (13:1) and another from the land (13:11).
symbols.cultural: The pose echoes the Colossus of Rhodes at the harbour mouth, an image of power over sea and land.
symbols.meaning: A claim of universal authority: the message is for the whole world. It also prepares for the counterfeit sovereignty of the beasts from sea and land in chapter 13.

readings.reading: Some preterists render "land" as the land of Israel, contrasted with the sea of the Gentile nations, both under the coming judgment and the new covenant.

symbols.phrase: He cried out with a loud voice like the roar of a lion
symbols.jewish: God roars like a lion from Zion in judgment (Amos 1:2; 3:8; Joel 3:16; Jeremiah 25:30) and also calls his scattered children home (Hosea 11:10-11). Amos 3:7-8 ties the lion's roar to prophecy: when the lion roars, who will not fear, and when the Lord speaks, who will not prophesy? 4 Ezra 11-12 has a lion (the Messiah) roar against the eagle (Rome).
symbols.meaning: An announcement with divine authority, inviting John's prophetic response (10:11). The Amos background links the roar to the revelation of God's secret to his servants the prophets (10:7).

symbols.phrase: The seven thunders spoke; "Seal up what they said and do not write it"
symbols.jewish: Psalm 29 describes the voice of the Lord seven times in the storm, thundering over the waters; thunder as God's voice appears in John 12:28-29 and Exodus 19:16-19. Daniel was told to seal up the vision (Daniel 8:26; 12:4, 9), and Paul heard things that cannot be told (2 Corinthians 12:4).
symbols.meaning: A further series of seven judgments or revelations that John is forbidden to record. Most interpreters take this to mean either that God has more judgments than are revealed, or (Bauckham, Beale) that a further series of warning judgments has been cancelled because, as the trumpets showed, warnings alone do not bring repentance; the next stage is the church's witness. The command reverses Daniel: what Daniel sealed is now open, but this part remains secret.

readings.reading: Elliott identified the seven thunders with the papal anathemas and bulls thundered against the Reformers, which the Reformers refused to accept as God's word.
Unrevealed future judgments in the Tribulation (Walvoord), reminding readers that not all is disclosed.
A reminder of the limits of revelation and/or the cancellation of further warning-judgments in favour of the church's witness (Bauckham, Beale).
Additional judgments on Jerusalem known to God but not recorded, or the sealing of matters not needed for the church's present task.

symbols.phrase: He lifted his right hand to heaven and swore by the one who lives forever, the Creator
keywords: swore by him who lives forever
symbols.jewish: Directly modelled on Daniel 12:7, where the man in linen raises both hands and swears by the one who lives forever that the end will come after a time, times and half a time. Raising the hand is an oath gesture (Genesis 14:22; Deuteronomy 32:40, where God swears by his own eternal life). The threefold Creator formula (heaven, earth, sea and all in them) recalls Exodus 20:11 and Nehemiah 9:6.
symbols.cultural: Oaths by the gods, and especially by the emperor's genius, were part of Roman civic and military life; here the oath is by the true Creator alone.
symbols.meaning: A solemn guarantee that God, as Creator, will complete his purpose for his creation. The oath ties the coming events to Daniel's three-and-a-half-year period, which chapter 11 develops.

symbols.phrase: There will be no more delay
symbols.jewish: Answers the martyrs' cry "How long?" (Revelation 6:10-11), where they were told to rest a little longer. Habakkuk 2:3 promises that the vision will not delay; 2 Baruch 20:1-2 and 4 Ezra 4:26 speak of the times hastening toward the end. Daniel 12:6 asked "How long until the end of these wonders?"
symbols.meaning: The Greek chronos ouketi estai means "there will be no more interval/delay", not "time will cease to exist" as the KJV phrase "time no longer" was sometimes taken. The period of waiting is over: the final events leading to the seventh trumpet are now under way.

readings.reading: The judgment on that generation is imminent (Matthew 24:34); there will be no further delay before Jerusalem's fall.
Signals the final, rapid progression of judgments in the second half of the Tribulation leading to Christ's return.
Some historicists read "time" (chronos) as a prophetic period and tied the oath to the Reformation era; Elliott read it as no more delay of the consummation once the last period begins.
The final stage of history before the consummation is announced; the church lives under the certainty that God will not delay beyond his appointed time.

symbols.phrase: The mystery of God will be fulfilled, as he proclaimed to his servants the prophets
symbols.jewish: Amos 3:7: the Lord does nothing without revealing his secret (sod) to his servants the prophets. Daniel 2:18-47 uses the Aramaic raz (mystery) for God's hidden plan of history, revealed to Daniel. At Qumran, raz nihyeh ("the mystery of what is to be") is a key term, and 1QpHab 7:1-5 says God revealed to the Teacher of Righteousness all the mysteries of the prophets' words. The verb "proclaimed" is literally "evangelized" (euangelizo).
symbols.meaning: God's long-hidden plan, announced by the prophets, of establishing his kingdom over the world through the Messiah, including the inclusion of the nations and the defeat of evil (compare Romans 16:25-26; Ephesians 3:3-6; Colossians 1:26-27). At the seventh trumpet the kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of God and his Christ (11:15).

readings.reading: The mystery includes the full revelation of the new covenant and the inclusion of the Gentiles, sealed by the end of the old covenant order in AD 70 (Ephesians 3).
God's purposes for the end of the age, completed when Christ returns to establish his millennial kingdom.
The consummation of God's kingdom at Christ's return, toward which the whole age moves.

symbols.phrase: Take it and eat it: sweet as honey in the mouth, bitter in the stomach
symbols.jewish: Ezekiel eats the scroll and finds it sweet as honey (Ezekiel 3:1-3), though its message is lament and woe and he goes away in bitterness (Ezekiel 3:14). Jeremiah ate God's words with joy (Jeremiah 15:16). God's words are sweeter than honey (Psalm 19:10; 119:103).
symbols.cultural: Ancient writers used eating as a metaphor for internalising teaching; Jewish children in later tradition were given honey on letters of the alphabet when beginning Torah study (a medieval custom, cited only as illustration).
symbols.meaning: Prophetic internalisation of God's word: receiving the revelation is sweet, but proclaiming its message of judgment, and the suffering it entails for the witnesses (11:7-10), is bitter. Some see the sweetness as the salvation of God's people and the bitterness as judgment on unbelievers.

readings.reading: The joy of the Reformers at receiving the Scriptures, followed by the bitterness of persecution, schism and religious wars (Elliott).
Sweet in the new covenant blessings it announces, bitter in the destruction of Jerusalem it foretells.
The prophetic word about the remaining judgments is sweet as God's word yet bitter in its content of woe (Walvoord).
The experience of every faithful witness: joy in God's word, sorrow in its rejection and in the suffering of proclaiming it.

symbols.phrase: You must prophesy again about many peoples, nations, tongues and kings
keywords: peoples and nations and tongues and kings
symbols.jewish: Jeremiah was appointed a prophet to nations and kingdoms (Jeremiah 1:10). The fourfold "peoples, nations, languages" echoes Daniel 3:4, 7; 5:19; 7:14, where it describes the empires and then the Son of Man's universal kingdom.
symbols.meaning: John's recommissioning: the second half of the book (chapters 11-22), or at least the following visions, is a renewed prophecy concerning the world's peoples and rulers. The preposition (epi) can mean "about" or "against", leaving open whether the prophecy is primarily judgment or witness for the nations.

readings.reading: After judging Israel, John prophesies concerning the Gentile nations and Rome (chapters 12-19).
Introduces the further prophecies about world rulers and the final empire (chapters 11-19).
Introduces a second, parallel account of church history (chapters 11-14 retracing the same period from the church's side).
The church's ongoing prophetic witness to the nations through the whole age.

The interlude introduces a new phase in the judgment of the first-century generation. The mighty angel (often Christ, as Chilton holds) stands over land (Israel) and sea (the nations), swearing that there will be no more delay: the judgment Jesus promised within a generation is about to fall. The little scroll is the covenant message John must proclaim, sweet in its new-covenant promise and bitter in its sentence on Jerusalem, and his recommissioning turns his prophecy toward the nations and Rome. This reading presupposes a pre-70 date, which is disputed.

The descending angel is Christ's intervention at the Reformation, after the Saracen and Turkish woes. The open little scroll is the Bible restored to the people through the printing press and vernacular translations; the seven thunders are the papal anathemas that the Reformers rejected; eating the scroll is the Reformers' joyful reception of Scripture, with the bitterness of persecution to follow; and "prophesy again" is the renewed preaching of the gospel to many nations (Elliott, Barnes).

The chapter is a parenthesis in the Tribulation between the sixth and seventh trumpets. A strong angel (not Christ) announces that the final judgments, culminating in the seventh trumpet and the bowls, will proceed without delay. The seven thunders are unrevealed judgments. The little scroll contains prophecies about the remaining events, which John must proclaim concerning the nations and kings of the end time (Walvoord, Thomas).

The chapter recommissions the church as a prophetic community. The glorious angel (perhaps the Angel of the Lord) gives John the scroll of God's redemptive plan, opened by the Lamb, and calls the church to internalise it and bear witness to the nations even at the cost of suffering. Because the trumpet warnings did not bring repentance (9:20-21), God turns from further warnings (the sealed thunders) to the witness of the church that follows in chapter 11 (Beale, Bauckham).

Many commentators blend approaches: the chapter echoes Daniel 12 and Ezekiel 2-3 to present John's renewed prophetic commission for his first-century audience, describes the mission of the church through history, and points to the still-future consummation at the seventh trumpet. Bauckham's argument that the scroll is the Lamb's scroll and that its message is the conversion of the nations through the church's witness has been influential across views.

questions: Is the mighty angel Christ or a created angel? What features of the text support each answer?
What does it mean that John was forbidden to write what the seven thunders said? How does this relate to Daniel 12:4 and Revelation 22:10?
Compare John's eating of the scroll with Ezekiel 2:8-3:3 and Jeremiah 15:16. Why is God's word both sweet and bitter for a prophet?
How does the "mystery of God" announced to the prophets (Revelation 10:7) relate to the kingdom proclaimed in Revelation 11:15 and to Paul's use of "mystery" in Ephesians 3?

title: Measuring the temple, the two witnesses and the seventh trumpet
section: The seven trumpets: interlude and seventh trumpet (Revelation 10:1-11:19)
summary: John is given a measuring rod and told to measure the temple of God, the altar and the worshippers, but to leave out the outer court, which is given to the nations to trample the holy city for 42 months. God's two witnesses, clothed in sackcloth and identified as the two olive trees and two lampstands of Zechariah 4, prophesy for 1,260 days with Elijah-like and Moses-like powers. When their testimony is finished, the beast from the Abyss kills them; their bodies lie unburied for three and a half days in the great city, spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified, while the world celebrates. Then God raises them, they ascend in a cloud, an earthquake strikes the city and the survivors give glory to God. The seventh trumpet sounds: heavenly voices proclaim that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and his Christ, the elders worship, and God's temple in heaven opens to reveal the ark of the covenant.

outline.heading: Measuring the temple; the outer court trampled for 42 months
The two witnesses and their powers
The witnesses killed by the beast; the world rejoices
Resurrection, ascension and earthquake; the survivors give glory to God
The second woe passes
Seventh trumpet: the kingdom proclaimed; the elders' thanksgiving
The heavenly temple opened and the ark of the covenant seen

context:
This is one of the most contested chapters in Revelation, and it carries weight in the debate about the book's date. The measuring of the temple draws on Ezekiel 40-48 (an angel measures an idealised temple) and Zechariah 2:1-5 (Jerusalem measured for protection), while measuring can also mark out for destruction (2 Samuel 8:2; 2 Kings 21:13; Lamentations 2:8). Herod's temple had a vast Court of the Gentiles, separated from the inner courts by a balustrade with Greek and Latin warnings forbidding foreigners entry on pain of death (two such inscriptions have been found). Jesus foretold that Jerusalem would be trampled by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled (Luke 21:24). The period of 42 months, 1,260 days and (in chapter 12) "a time, times and half a time" comes from Daniel 7:25 and 12:7, Daniel's measure for the persecution of the saints, historically associated with Antiochus IV's desecration of the temple (167-164 BC, 1 Maccabees 1-4). It also echoes the three and a half years of drought under Elijah (Luke 4:25; James 5:17).

Partial preterists (notably Gentry, Before Jerusalem Fell) argue that a command to measure a still-standing temple implies the book was written before AD 70, and that the 42 months match the Roman campaign from spring 67 to August 70. Most scholars, who date Revelation to about AD 95, reply that John's temple is symbolic (as elsewhere in Revelation, 3:12; 21:22) or that he reuses an older oracle, and that the date question cannot rest on this passage. The two witnesses combine Moses (water to blood, plagues) and Elijah (fire from heaven, shutting the sky), the figures expected at the end in Malachi 4:5 and seen with Jesus on the mountain of transfiguration; early Christian writers (Hippolytus, Tertullian) often identified them as Enoch and Elijah, who never died. The "great city" that is spiritually Sodom and Egypt and where the Lord was crucified invites identification with Jerusalem, though many argue it is Babylon/Rome or the world city. The seventh trumpet then leaps to the consummation, with language from Psalm 2 and Daniel 7, and the ark, lost since the Babylonian destruction of 587 BC and said in 2 Maccabees 2:4-8 to have been hidden by Jeremiah until God gathers his people, appears in the heavenly temple.

symbols.phrase: A measuring rod like a staff: measure the temple of God, the altar and the worshippers
symbols.jewish: In Ezekiel 40:3-42:20 a man with a measuring reed measures the future temple, a sign of its restoration and holiness; in Zechariah 2:1-5 Jerusalem is measured as a promise of protection, with God as a wall of fire. Measuring can also mean marking out for judgment (2 Samuel 8:2; 2 Kings 21:13; Amos 7:7-9; Lamentations 2:8). 1 Enoch 61:1-5 has angels take measuring cords to measure the righteous, signifying preservation. Revelation 21:15-17 measures the New Jerusalem.
symbols.cultural: Surveyors with measuring rods (Greek kalamos, a reed of about 3 metres) laid out cities, temples and land boundaries in the Roman world.
symbols.meaning: Measuring here most likely signifies protection and ownership: God guards his true sanctuary and worshippers. What exactly the temple, altar and worshippers represent is disputed.

readings.reading: A command concerning the literal Herodian temple still standing when John wrote, separating the faithful remnant (the inner sanctuary, i.e. the true worshippers, the church) from the apostate city given to the Romans (Gentry, Chilton).
A future rebuilt temple in Jerusalem during the Tribulation, measured to mark it for God's evaluation and the protection of a believing Jewish remnant (Walvoord, Thomas).
The Reformers' re-establishment of true worship and doctrine, measuring the church by the rule of Scripture and excluding the outer court of nominal (papal) Christendom.
The church as God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21), spiritually protected even while physically persecuted (Beale, Hendriksen).

symbols.phrase: The temple of God and the altar
symbols.jewish: The word naos refers to the inner sanctuary (Holy Place and Holy of Holies), not the whole temple complex (hieron). In Revelation, the naos is usually the heavenly sanctuary (7:15; 11:19; 15:5) and believers are pillars in it (3:12); in the New Jerusalem there is no temple, because God and the Lamb are its temple (21:22). The altar may be the incense altar of 8:3-5 or the altar of burnt offering under which the martyrs cry (6:9).
symbols.cultural: Temples (naoi) of the imperial cult stood in Ephesus, Pergamum and Smyrna, the contrast between God's true sanctuary and the emperor's being sharp for Asian readers.
symbols.meaning: The sanctuary of God's presence, whose identity depends on the interpretive approach. The worshippers being counted suggests that it is people, not merely a building, that God preserves.

readings.reading: Gentry argues the Jerusalem temple was standing, so the book predates AD 70; the inner sanctuary stands for the faithful (Christian) remnant within Israel. Critics reply that the language is visionary and symbolic and that John's readers in Asia were far from the Jerusalem temple.
A literal third temple rebuilt in Jerusalem, to be desecrated by the Antichrist (Daniel 9:27; 2 Thessalonians 2:4).
The church, God's spiritual temple, where true worship takes place.
The true, spiritual church as distinguished from the outward ecclesiastical system.

symbols.phrase: The court outside the temple, given to the nations
symbols.jewish: Herod's temple had a large outer court, the Court of the Gentiles, where non-Jews could enter; a stone barrier (soreg) with inscriptions forbade them to go further on pain of death (Josephus, Jewish War 5.5.2; Antiquities 15.11.5; two inscriptions survive). Ezekiel 44:7-9 condemns bringing foreigners into the sanctuary. Jesus foretold that Jerusalem would be trampled by Gentiles (Luke 21:24).
symbols.cultural: During the Roman siege in AD 70, rival Jewish factions held the inner temple courts while the Romans eventually burned the outer porticoes and entered the courts (Josephus, Jewish War 6.2-6.4).
symbols.meaning: The outer court represents what God permits to be overrun or persecuted; the contrast between measured (protected) inner sanctuary and unmeasured (exposed) outer court is the key to interpretation.

readings.reading: The literal outer court and city of Jerusalem, given over to Roman armies (Luke 21:20-24), in contrast to the preserved spiritual remnant.
The literal court of a future temple, given to Gentile domination during the second half of the Tribulation.
The outward visible church overrun by corruption, the papal system "trampling" the church for 1,260 years.
The church's external, physical existence, exposed to persecution, while its inner spiritual life is secure (Beale).

symbols.phrase: They will trample the holy city
symbols.jewish: Jerusalem is the holy city (Isaiah 52:1; Nehemiah 11:1; Matthew 4:5). Its trampling by nations is a lament in Isaiah 63:18, Psalm 79:1, Daniel 8:13 (the sanctuary and host trampled under Antiochus) and 1 Maccabees 3:45, 51; 4:60. Luke 21:24 is the nearest parallel.
symbols.meaning: An image of the people of God, or of their city, under hostile power for a limited time. Elsewhere in Revelation "the holy city" is the New Jerusalem (21:2, 10; 22:19), which suggests to many that here, too, it means God's people rather than the earthly Jerusalem.

readings.reading: Literal Jerusalem, besieged and trampled by Rome in AD 67-70, as Jesus foretold in Luke 21:24.
Literal Jerusalem during the future Tribulation, under the Antichrist's domination.
The church, which suffers persecution throughout the age.
The true church oppressed under papal domination for 1,260 years.

symbols.phrase: 42 months; 1,260 days
symbols.jewish: Daniel 7:25 and 12:7 limit the persecution of the saints to "a time, times and half a time" (three and a half years); Daniel 9:27 speaks of the covenant broken in the middle of the week; Daniel 12:11-12 has 1,290 and 1,335 days. The period evokes Antiochus IV's persecution and temple desecration (167-164 BC) and Elijah's three-and-a-half-year drought (Luke 4:25; James 5:17). Israel's wilderness journey had 42 stages (Numbers 33). Revelation uses all three forms (11:2-3; 12:6, 14; 13:5).
symbols.meaning: The time of the church's (or God's people's) persecution and witness, limited by God. Half of seven, it signals a broken, incomplete period of evil. Its relation to Daniel's seventieth week is a major dividing line among views.

readings.reading: The literal period of the Roman war against Judea, from Vespasian's commission in early AD 67 to the fall of the temple in August 70 (about 42 months), as argued by Gentry.
The literal second half (or, for the witnesses, perhaps the first half) of Daniel's seventieth week, a future seven-year Tribulation (Walvoord, Thomas).
By the year-for-a-day principle, 1,260 years of papal supremacy, variously dated (e.g. 533/538 to 1793/1798, with the French Revolution and Napoleon's capture of Pope Pius VI in 1798 often cited).
The whole period between Christ's first and second comings, during which the church both witnesses and suffers (Beale, Hendriksen).
