The 1,260 days fit within the generation ending in AD 70, as in partial preterism, with the seventh trumpet that follows read as the consummation also fulfilled then.

symbols.phrase: My two witnesses
symbols.jewish: Valid testimony required two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15; Numbers 35:30; Matthew 18:16); Jesus sent disciples out two by two (Luke 10:1). Moses and Elijah, the law and the prophets, appear with Jesus at the transfiguration (Mark 9:4), and Jewish tradition expected Elijah's return before the Day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5-6; Sirach 48:10) and a prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15). Zechariah 4 has two anointed ones (Joshua the high priest and Zerubbabel the governor). Qumran anticipated two messiahs, of Aaron and of Israel (1QS 9:11). Early Christian writers often expected Enoch and Elijah to return (Hippolytus, On Christ and Antichrist 43; Tertullian, On the Soul 50).
symbols.meaning: Prophetic witnesses empowered by God to testify during the period of trampling. The question of whether they are two individuals or a symbol of the witnessing community is central. Their description as lampstands (cf. 1:20, where lampstands are churches) inclines many to the corporate reading.

readings.reading: Two literal individuals in the future Tribulation, often Moses and Elijah (Walvoord leans this way) or Enoch and Elijah, or two prophets in their spirit.

Interpretations vary: the faithful Christian witness in Jerusalem before AD 70 (Chilton, typified by the law and prophets), or particular apostles or leaders (some suggest Peter and Paul, or James the Just and another) killed in that era.

The faithful witnesses against Rome through the 1,260 years of papal dominance, such as the Waldenses, Albigenses, Wycliffe and Hus; their "death" and "resurrection" is applied to the suppression of dissent before the Fifth Lateran Council (1512-1517) and Luther's posting of the theses three and a half years later (Elliott).

The whole church in its prophetic witness (two for legal testimony, and because only two of the seven churches in chapters 2-3 were wholly faithful), suffering and yet vindicated (Beale, Hendriksen, Bauckham).

symbols.phrase: Clothed in sackcloth
symbols.jewish: Sackcloth, a coarse dark cloth of goat or camel hair, was worn in mourning and repentance (Genesis 37:34; Jonah 3:5-8; Daniel 9:3; Matthew 11:21). Elijah wore a hairy garment (2 Kings 1:8) and prophets were known by rough garments (Zechariah 13:4; Mark 1:6 for John the Baptist).
symbols.meaning: The witnesses call for repentance and mourn the sin and coming judgment of those they address; their garb identifies them as prophets in the line of Elijah and John the Baptist.

symbols.phrase: The two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth
symbols.jewish: Zechariah 4:2-14 sees a golden lampstand fed by two olive trees, interpreted as the "two anointed ones" (literally "sons of oil") who stand by the Lord of the whole earth, namely Joshua the high priest and Zerubbabel the Davidic governor, who rebuilt the temple "not by might nor by power, but by my Spirit" (Zechariah 4:6). In Revelation 1:20 lampstands are churches. Olive oil fuelled the temple menorah (Exodus 27:20).
symbols.meaning: The witnesses are Spirit-empowered bearers of priestly and royal testimony, like Joshua and Zerubbabel who rebuilt the temple. John adapts one lampstand into two, which supports the view that they represent the witnessing church (lampstands) in its royal-priestly calling (1:6; 5:10).

readings.reading: The church in its kingly and priestly witness, sustained by the Spirit (Beale).
Two individual prophets empowered by the Holy Spirit in the Tribulation.
The witnessing church (or its leaders) as the true priesthood and kingship in contrast to Jerusalem's apostate leaders.

symbols.phrase: Fire comes from their mouths and consumes their enemies
symbols.jewish: Elijah called down fire on the soldiers of Ahaziah (2 Kings 1:10-12); God made Jeremiah's words a fire that consumes the people (Jeremiah 5:14); Sirach 48:1-3 says Elijah arose like fire and his word burned like a torch. 4 Ezra 13:10 has the Messiah destroy enemies with a stream of fire from his mouth.
symbols.meaning: The witnesses' prophetic word carries God's judgment on those who reject it; the fire comes from their mouths, i.e. their testimony. Most see it as figurative (the power of the word), though some futurists take it literally.

readings.reading: Literal miraculous fire defending the witnesses during their ministry.
The power of the gospel word to pronounce judgment on those who oppose it.

symbols.phrase: Power to shut the sky, turn waters to blood and strike the earth with plagues
symbols.jewish: Elijah shut the heavens for three and a half years (1 Kings 17:1; 18:1; Luke 4:25; James 5:17). Moses turned the Nile to blood and struck Egypt with plagues (Exodus 7:17-20; 1 Samuel 4:8).
symbols.meaning: The witnesses carry on the ministries of Moses and Elijah: confronting an oppressive and idolatrous power, calling God's people out of bondage and proclaiming judgment. The plagues link them to the trumpet plagues just described.

readings.reading: Literal miraculous powers in the Tribulation; some (Walvoord) see the two as Moses and Elijah themselves.
The church's prophetic witness has power to bring God's judgments, as the trumpets show (Beale).
Figurative of the spiritual power of the faithful witnesses' testimony against the corrupt church.

symbols.phrase: The beast that comes up from the Abyss will make war on them
keywords: beast that comes up from the abyss
symbols.jewish: The first mention of "the beast", introduced as if already known. It draws on Daniel 7:3, 7 (beasts from the sea) and 7:21, where the little horn wages war against the saints and prevails until the Ancient of Days comes. The Abyss connects it to the demonic origin of 9:1-11; in 17:8 the beast "was, and is not, and is about to come up from the Abyss".
symbols.cultural: For many scholars the beast's ascent from the Abyss after death reflects the Nero redivivus legend, the belief that Nero would return after his death in AD 68 (Tacitus, Histories 2.8; Suetonius, Nero 57).
symbols.meaning: The persecuting power, energised by Satan, which seems to triumph over God's witnesses. It anticipates the fuller portrait of chapters 13 and 17.

readings.reading: Rome under Nero (who persecuted the church and began the Jewish War), or the Jewish authorities allied with Rome; Gentry identifies the beast with Nero/Rome.
The future Antichrist, a world ruler who kills the two witnesses in the middle or end of the Tribulation.
The papacy (or the papal power with its secular allies) suppressing the witnesses.
Satanic persecuting power embodied in states and systems throughout history, culminating before the end.

symbols.phrase: The great city, spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified
symbols.jewish: Prophets called Jerusalem "Sodom" when it was unfaithful (Isaiah 1:9-10; Jeremiah 23:14; Ezekiel 16:46-56). Egypt is the archetypal oppressor and place of bondage (Exodus 1-14). Jerusalem killed the prophets (Matthew 23:37; Luke 13:33-34), and Jesus was crucified outside its walls (Hebrews 13:12). The adverb pneumatikos ("spiritually", "prophetically", BSB "figuratively") signals a symbolic, Spirit-given name.
symbols.meaning: The "great city" in Revelation elsewhere always refers to Babylon (16:19; 17:18; 18:10-21), which many identify with Rome. The reference to the crucifixion suggests Jerusalem, so interpreters divide: Jerusalem, Rome, or the world-city of rebellious humanity that includes both. Which city is meant is a disputed matter.

readings.reading: Literal Jerusalem, which killed the Lord and his prophets and is about to be judged (Chilton, Gentry); the identification also supports reading "Babylon" in chapters 17-18 as Jerusalem (a minority view even among scholars).
Literal Jerusalem in the Tribulation, morally degraded and allied with the Antichrist (Walvoord, Thomas).
Papal Rome or the territory of Latin Christendom, spiritually Sodom and Egypt, where Christ was crucified afresh in his members.
The world-city of humanity in rebellion against God (Babylon), which includes Jerusalem's rejection of Jesus; it is everywhere the church suffers (Beale, Bauckham).

symbols.phrase: Their bodies lie in the street and are not permitted burial
symbols.jewish: Denial of burial was a supreme disgrace and curse in Israel (Deuteronomy 28:26; Psalm 79:2-3, lamenting the dead of Jerusalem left unburied by the nations; Jeremiah 8:1-2; 16:4). Tobit risked his life to bury executed Jews (Tobit 1:17-19; 2:3-8).
symbols.cultural: Leaving enemies unburied was a deliberate humiliation in the Greco-Roman world (the Antigone story is the classic example); executed criminals were often denied burial, and crucified bodies were left on crosses.
symbols.meaning: The world's utmost contempt for the witnesses: total public humiliation, exposed to "peoples, tribes, languages and nations" (11:9), which points beyond a single local event to a universal scene.

readings.reading: A literal public display, which some futurists suggest would be visible worldwide through modern media.
The apparent defeat and public shaming of the church at the end of the age.

symbols.phrase: Three and a half days
symbols.jewish: A brief counterpart to the 1,260 days of witness: the witnesses' public ministry lasts three and a half years, their apparent defeat three and a half days. It recalls Jesus' death and resurrection after three days and Daniel's half-week.
symbols.meaning: A short time of apparent triumph for evil, contrasted with the longer period of witness; the death of the witnesses is real but brief, and vindication follows.

readings.reading: Three and a half years, by the day-year principle, from the Fifth Lateran Council's declaration of victory over dissent (May 1514) to Luther's Ninety-Five Theses (October 1517), a match Elliott emphasized.
A literal three and a half days.
A short period of apparent triumph over the church immediately before Christ's return.

symbols.phrase: Those who dwell on the earth gloat, celebrate and send one another gifts
symbols.jewish: An inverted Purim: in Esther 9:19, 22 the Jews celebrated deliverance from their enemies by sending portions to one another; here the persecutors celebrate the death of God's witnesses. Compare also Nehemiah 8:10-12.
symbols.cultural: Gift exchange marked Roman festivals such as the Saturnalia and imperial celebrations of victories.
symbols.meaning: The world's relief at being freed from the prophets' unwelcome testimony ("these two prophets had tormented them"), a parody of godly celebration. It shows how deeply the message of repentance was resented.

symbols.phrase: The breath of life from God entered them and they stood on their feet
symbols.jewish: Ezekiel 37:5, 10: in the valley of dry bones, breath enters the slain and they stand on their feet, a vision of Israel's national restoration. Genesis 2:7 has God breathe life into Adam.
symbols.meaning: The vindication and resurrection of the witnesses. Whether this is a literal bodily resurrection of two individuals, the final resurrection of the church, or a figure for the revival of the church's witness depends on the overall approach.

readings.reading: Literal resurrection and ascension of the two witnesses near the end of the Tribulation.
The revival of Protestant witness at the Reformation, or later restoration of liberty to Protestants.
The vindication of the church at Christ's return (the resurrection of the righteous), or more generally God's pattern of reviving his witness after apparent defeat.
The vindication of the martyred witnesses and the church's triumph over Jerusalem, sometimes linked to the safety of the church after the city's fall.

symbols.phrase: "Come up here" — they went up to heaven in a cloud
keywords: went up to heaven in a cloud
symbols.jewish: Elijah was taken up to heaven in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:11); Jewish tradition held that Moses too was taken up (the lost Assumption of Moses; Josephus, Antiquities 4.326 says a cloud came over him). Jesus ascended in a cloud (Acts 1:9-11). John himself heard "Come up here" in Revelation 4:1.
symbols.meaning: Public vindication: the enemies see the witnesses honoured by God, as Jesus' enemies will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds (1:7). The witnesses follow the pattern of their Lord: witness, death, resurrection, ascension.

readings.reading: A literal ascension of the two witnesses; some (e.g. some mid-tribulationists) connect it with a rapture of believers, but most dispensationalists place the rapture before the Tribulation (Revelation 4:1 is often read as its symbol).
The church's exaltation at the end, possibly corresponding to 1 Thessalonians 4:17.

symbols.phrase: A great earthquake: a tenth of the city fell, seven thousand killed
symbols.jewish: Ezekiel 38:19-20 has a great earthquake in the land at God's final judgment; Amos 5:3 says a city that marches out a thousand will be left with a hundred (a tenth). Elijah was told that God kept 7,000 who had not bowed to Baal (1 Kings 19:18), so the number reverses Elijah's remnant: now 7,000 die and the majority are converted.
symbols.cultural: Earthquakes repeatedly destroyed cities in Asia Minor (Sardis AD 17; Laodicea c. AD 60).
symbols.meaning: A limited judgment (a tenth, not a third or all) that, unlike the trumpets, results in the majority repenting. Bauckham argues this is the key reversal of the book: where judgment alone failed (9:20-21), the witness of the church, vindicated by God, leads the nations to give glory to God.

readings.reading: Upheaval in Jerusalem in the war years; some note Josephus's report of an earthquake and storm in AD 68 (Jewish War 4.4.5). Interpreters differ on whether the survivors' response is genuine conversion.
A literal earthquake in Jerusalem near the end of the Tribulation.
The political upheaval of the Reformation era or the French Revolution, in which a "tenth" kingdom of the papal realm fell (often France).
A partial judgment that, with the church's vindicated witness, brings many to repentance.

symbols.phrase: The rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven
keywords: gave glory to the god of heaven
symbols.jewish: "Give glory to God" can be a call to confession and repentance (Joshua 7:19; Jeremiah 13:16), and in Revelation it is the response of repentance (14:7; 16:9, where the lack of it is condemned). "God of heaven" is a Persian-era title in Daniel 2:18-19, 37, 44, Ezra and Nehemiah, used by Gentile kings who acknowledge Israel's God (Daniel 4:34-37).
symbols.meaning: Whether this is genuine conversion or merely forced acknowledgment is disputed. Bauckham, Caird and others argue for true repentance, since 14:7 and 16:9 equate "giving glory" with repentance; Beale, Thomas and others think it may be coerced recognition, like Nebuchadnezzar's.

readings.reading: Bauckham and Sweet: a picture of the conversion of the nations through the church's faithful witness, the great hope of Revelation.
Thomas and Walvoord: likely the conversion of a remnant in Jerusalem, perhaps connected with the salvation of Israel (Romans 11:26), though some say it is only fearful acknowledgment.
Varies: either superficial fear in Jerusalem, or the conversion of many Jews who acknowledged Christ after the judgments.

symbols.phrase: The second woe has passed; the third woe is coming soon
symbols.jewish: Continues the woe-oracle structure of 8:13 and 9:12.
symbols.meaning: Ties the interlude (10:1-11:13) to the sixth trumpet. The third woe is not explicitly identified; most link it to the seventh trumpet and the judgments it opens, including the devil's rage on the earth (12:12) and the bowls (15-16).

symbols.phrase: The seventh trumpet: the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ
keywords: kingdom of our lord and of his christ
symbols.jewish: Psalm 2:2 speaks of the Lord and his anointed (Christ), against whom the nations rage; Daniel 2:44 and 7:14, 18, 27 promise an everlasting kingdom given to the Son of Man and the saints; Exodus 15:18 ends the song of the sea with the Lord reigning forever; Obadiah 21 and Zechariah 14:9 foresee the Lord as king over all the earth. Trumpets were sounded at royal enthronements (1 Kings 1:34, 39; 2 Kings 9:13).
symbols.cultural: Emperors claimed kingship over the oikoumene, the inhabited world; coins and inscriptions proclaimed Caesar's reign as a gift of the gods. The heavenly announcement asserts that world rule belongs to God and his Messiah.
symbols.meaning: The climax of the trumpets and of the mystery of God (10:7). The singular "kingdom" stresses that world rule passes entirely to God and Christ. The nature and timing of this transfer is the central millennial question in this chapter.

readings.reading: The decisive transfer of the kingdom at Christ's ascension and its public vindication in AD 70, after which the kingdom grows through the church until the final consummation (Gentry, Chilton).
Anticipates Christ's literal return and earthly reign; dispensationalists see the reign beginning at the second coming after the Tribulation, followed by the millennium (Walvoord).
The final establishment of Christ's kingdom after the overthrow of the papal and Turkish powers, often expected in the near future of the commentator.
The consummation of the kingdom at Christ's return at the end of history (Beale, Hendriksen); the seventh trumpet parallels the seventh seal and bowl.

The full arrival of the kingdom and the "last trumpet" (1 Corinthians 15:52) in AD 70. This places the view outside creedal orthodoxy, since the creeds confess a future return and bodily resurrection; proponents argue that the New Testament's time statements require it.

symbols.phrase: The twenty-four elders fall on their faces and give thanks
symbols.jewish: The elders recall the twenty-four priestly divisions (1 Chronicles 24:7-19) and the elders of Israel before God (Isaiah 24:23); their prostration and hymn follow temple patterns of thanksgiving (todah). "Lord God Almighty" (Pantokrator) renders the Septuagint's title for the Lord of hosts (Amos 4:13).
symbols.cultural: Prostration (proskynesis) before rulers was a feature of eastern and later imperial court ceremony; Domitian reportedly liked to be addressed as "Lord and God" (Suetonius, Domitian 13).
symbols.meaning: The heavenly court responds to the kingdom proclamation with thanksgiving, affirming that God has taken his great power and begun to reign.

symbols.phrase: The one who is and who was (no longer "who is to come")
symbols.jewish: The threefold title of 1:4, 8 and 4:8 (who was, and is, and is to come) echoes Exodus 3:14 as expanded in Jewish tradition; the Palestinian Targum (Pseudo-Jonathan) on Deuteronomy 32:39 and Exodus 3:14 develops a similar three-tense formula (a later text, reflecting earlier traditions).
symbols.cultural: Greek religious formulas spoke of Zeus who was, is and will be (Pausanias 10.12.10), which Revelation adapts for Israel's God.
symbols.meaning: The omission of "who is to come" here and in 16:5 is deliberate: from the perspective of the seventh trumpet, God has come and begun to reign. It signals that the seventh trumpet depicts the consummation.

readings.reading: God's "coming" in judgment in AD 70 established his reign in a decisive new way, while a final coming remains (for partial preterists) future.
Anticipates the second coming at the end of the Tribulation.
The final coming of God at the end of history (Beale, Bauckham).

symbols.phrase: The nations raged, your wrath came; the time to judge the dead and reward your servants
symbols.jewish: Psalm 2:1, 5, 12 (the nations rage and God speaks in wrath) and Psalm 99:1 in the Greek translation (the Lord reigns, let the peoples be angry). Daniel 12:2 speaks of the resurrection of the dead for judgment and reward; Psalm 115:13 blesses those who fear the Lord, small and great. Amos 3:7 calls the prophets God's servants.
symbols.meaning: A summary of the final events: the nations' rebellion, God's wrath, the judgment of the dead, and the reward of prophets, saints and God-fearers. It previews chapters 19-20, especially the last judgment (20:11-15).

readings.reading: Most postmillennialists (and partial preterists) take 11:18 as a proleptic summary of the final judgment at the end of history, after the kingdom has grown through the gospel; some partial preterists see a first-century foreshadowing in AD 70.
The final judgment at Christ's single return, parallel to Revelation 20:11-15, supporting the recapitulation structure of the book.

The judgment of the dead mentioned here is anticipatory; the rewards are given at various stages (at the judgment seat of Christ, after the Tribulation, and the great white throne after the millennium).
Anticipates both the rewards at Christ's return and, after the millennium, the final judgment, summarised together.
The judgment of the dead took place in the spiritual realm in AD 70 (Max King, Don Preston); critics say this denies the future judgment of the creeds.

symbols.phrase: To destroy those who destroy the earth
keywords: destroy those who destroy the earth
symbols.jewish: A wordplay on diaphtheirō (ruin, corrupt). Genesis 6:11-13 (in the Greek translation) says the earth was corrupted and God would destroy it with the corrupters; Jeremiah 51:25 calls Babylon a "destroying mountain" that corrupts the whole earth. Jubilees and 1 Enoch associate the watchers' corruption of the earth with the flood judgment.
symbols.cultural: Imperial propaganda presented Rome as the bringer of peace and prosperity (Pax Romana); Revelation inverts this, calling Rome (Babylon) the corrupter of the earth (19:2).
symbols.meaning: God's judgment is fitting retribution (lex talionis) on those who ruin his creation and its peoples, especially the beast and Babylon (19:2). It affirms God's commitment to his creation rather than its abandonment.

symbols.phrase: God's temple in heaven opened and the ark of his covenant seen
symbols.jewish: The ark, symbol of God's presence and covenant, kept in the Holy of Holies (Exodus 25:10-22; Leviticus 16:2), disappeared at the Babylonian destruction of 587 BC; the Second Temple's Holy of Holies was empty (Josephus, Jewish War 5.5.5; Pompey found it so in 63 BC, Tacitus, Histories 5.9). 2 Maccabees 2:4-8 relates that Jeremiah hid the ark until God would gather his people again, and 2 Baruch 6:7-10 has an angel hide the temple vessels until the restoration. Jeremiah 3:16 says that in the future the ark will no longer be remembered.
symbols.cultural: Pagan temples hid their most sacred objects in the inner adyton, to be seen only on special festival days when the doors were opened.
symbols.meaning: God's covenant presence, unseen in the earthly sanctuary, is revealed in heaven: his covenant faithfulness to his people is the ground of the coming judgments and of their salvation. The lightning, thunder, earthquake and hail end the trumpet series and anticipate the bowls (16:18-21), and the heavenly temple frames the next section (chapters 12-14).

readings.reading: The heavenly reality supersedes the earthly temple about to be destroyed in AD 70: access to God's presence is now through the heavenly sanctuary (Hebrews 9:11-12; Chilton).
A heavenly sanctuary from which the final judgments proceed; some popular futurists link it to speculation about the recovery of the literal ark, which most scholars reject.
Revelation of God's covenant presence, guaranteeing the salvation of his people at the consummation and introducing a new cycle of visions.

symbols.phrase: Lightning, rumblings, thunder, an earthquake and great hail
symbols.jewish: The Sinai storm theophany (Exodus 19:16-19), with hail added from the Egyptian plague (Exodus 9:23-24) and Joshua's battle (Joshua 10:11). The formula expands from 8:5 and anticipates 16:18-21.
symbols.meaning: The end of the trumpet series in the final theophany of judgment; the escalating formula ties together the ends of the seals (8:5), trumpets (11:19) and bowls (16:18-21).

readings.reading: Supports recapitulation: each series ends at the final judgment (Bauckham, Beale).
Literal phenomena in the final stage of the Tribulation, in a progressive sequence.

Revelation 11 is a key text for the pre-70 dating and preterist reading (Gentry, Before Jerusalem Fell; Chilton, Days of Vengeance). The temple still stands and John measures its inner sanctuary (the faithful remnant) while the outer court and holy city are handed to the Roman armies for the 42 months of the Jewish War (AD 67-70), as Jesus foretold in Luke 21:24. The great city "where their Lord was crucified" is Jerusalem; the two witnesses are the church's witness in Jerusalem (variously identified). The seventh trumpet announces the kingdom of God, decisively established in Christ's ascension and vindicated by the judgment on Jerusalem, and continuing until the final judgment. Most scholars, who date Revelation to c. AD 95, regard the temple language as symbolic and dispute this dating argument.

Full preterists accept the first-century reading of the temple, the 42 months and the great city, but also take the seventh trumpet as the "last trumpet" of 1 Corinthians 15:52, so that the resurrection, judgment of the dead and full arrival of the kingdom took place (spiritually) in AD 70 (Max King, Don Preston). This places the view outside the creeds, which confess a future bodily resurrection and final judgment; proponents reply that the time statements of the New Testament require it, while critics (including partial preterists such as Gentry) argue that it confuses a covenantal judgment with the end of history.

The chapter traces the true church through the 1,260 years of papal supremacy. Measuring the temple is the Reformation's restoration of true worship by the rule of Scripture, with the outer court representing nominal Christendom. The two witnesses are the faithful minority who testified against Rome across the centuries (Waldenses, Wycliffe, Hus); their apparent death and three-and-a-half-day exposure correspond to the suppression of dissent proclaimed at the Fifth Lateran Council (1514), and their resurrection to Luther's Reformation (1517). The earthquake and fall of a tenth of the city are often applied to the Reformation or the French Revolution, and the seventh trumpet looks to the final triumph of Christ (Elliott, Barnes).

A rebuilt temple will stand in Jerusalem during the Tribulation; it is measured while the city is trampled by Gentiles for 42 months under the Antichrist. Two literal prophets (perhaps Moses and Elijah, or Enoch and Elijah) minister for 1,260 days with miraculous powers, are killed by the Antichrist in Jerusalem, lie unburied for three and a half literal days while the world watches, and are raised and taken to heaven. A great earthquake strikes Jerusalem, and survivors acknowledge God. The seventh trumpet anticipates Christ's return to set up his literal kingdom (Walvoord, Thomas).

The temple is the church, measured (protected) in its spiritual life while its outward existence is trampled throughout the church age (the 42 months). The two witnesses are the witnessing church, in the roles of Moses and Elijah, the royal priesthood of Zechariah 4; they suffer, appear to be defeated at the end by the beast, but are raised and vindicated. The great city is the world-system in rebellion. The response of the survivors in 11:13 portrays the conversion of the nations through the church's faithful witness. The seventh trumpet is the last judgment and consummation (Hendriksen, Beale, Bauckham).

Many recent commentators blend approaches. Osborne and Ladd, for example, see a future fulfilment involving literal Jerusalem and perhaps two individual prophets, while also seeing the witnesses as models for the church's witness in every age. Bauckham and Koester stress first-century resonances (the trampled city, Nero's persecution, the imperial claims) along with the symbolic nature of the measures and the universal scope of the church's witness.

Postmillennialists emphasize that the seventh trumpet proclaims a kingdom already given to Christ at his ascension (Daniel 7:13-14; Matthew 28:18) and that the church's witness (11:13) leads to the conversion of the nations. Partial preterist postmillennialists see AD 70 as the public vindication of the kingdom, after which it grows through the gospel until the final judgment summarised in 11:18.

Amillennialists read 11:15-19 as the end of history: the seventh trumpet is the last trumpet, the consummation of the kingdom and the final judgment, parallel to the end of the seals (6:12-17) and the bowls (16:17-21). The witnesses' 1,260 days are the church age, with the beast's war on them corresponding to the final rebellion of 20:7-10 (Beale, Hendriksen, Riddlebarger).

Historic premillennialists (Ladd) see the seventh trumpet as anticipating Christ's return, after which he reigns on earth during the millennium (Revelation 20) before the final judgment; 11:15-18 compresses these stages into a single announcement. Ladd held that the passage may point to the future conversion of Israel (Romans 11:26).

Dispensational premillennialists place the chapter in the future seven-year Tribulation, which is Daniel's seventieth week, with a rebuilt temple and two literal prophets; the seventh trumpet announces Christ's return at the end of the Tribulation to establish the millennial kingdom from Jerusalem. They usually distinguish this trumpet from the "last trumpet" of 1 Corinthians 15:52, which they connect with a pretribulational rapture (Walvoord, Thomas).

questions: What does the act of measuring signify in Ezekiel 40, Zechariah 2 and Amos 7? Which background best fits Revelation 11:1-2, and why?
Are the two witnesses two individuals or a symbol of the witnessing church? Weigh the clues: lampstands (Revelation 1:20), Moses and Elijah, worldwide audience (11:9).
How does the reference to the great city "where their Lord was crucified" affect the identity of the city, and how does that connect to Babylon in Revelation 17-18?
Compare 9:20-21 (no repentance after the trumpets) with 11:13 (people give glory to God after the witnesses' vindication). What does this contrast suggest about how God brings the nations to himself?
How do the millennial views interpret the seventh trumpet and the proclamation of the kingdom in Revelation 11:15? What would each say about the time of its fulfilment?
